summary: This Standards Track document defines the BGP Link Bandwidth Extended Community, which carries bandwidth information so routers can do weighted load balancing across multiple paths. It specifies the format and processing rules.

eli5.summary: Roads of different sizes get a sign telling how much traffic they hold, so cars are shared out fairly.

questions: what is the bgp link bandwidth extended community
how does bgp weighted load balancing work
what is the link bandwidth subtype 0x04
subtitle: A BGP extended community that tells routers how much bandwidth is behind a path, so traffic can be shared in proportion.

tldr.problem: Equal load-balancing across BGP paths ignores that the paths can have different capacities.
tldr.mechanism: The Link Bandwidth Extended Community carries a bandwidth value in bytes per second, as a 32-bit IEEE floating point number, in either a transitive or a non-transitive form. Receivers can use the values or their ratio as load-balancing weights.
tldr.outcome: Routers can do weighted load-balancing over multiple paths. The RFC fixes the format and the sender, receiver and re-advertisement rules, and leaves the weighting details to other documents.

today: RFC 10005 is a Proposed Standard published in June 2026. The unit metadata lists no obsoleting or updating RFC, so it is the current definition of the Link Bandwidth Extended Community.

sections.title: Unequal Paths, Equal Shares
sections.content:
Traditional equal load-balancing does not account for the varying capacities of different paths. This RFC defines a BGP extended community (the mechanism from RFC 4360) that carries the bandwidth information of a directly connected link, or of a multi-hop or multipath next hop, as advertised by a router. It comes in a transitive and a non-transitive variant.

Other routers can then use this information to maximize utilization of network resources. The RFC defines only the format and the processing rules. How the weights are used and how the bandwidth is computed are left to other documents.
sections.eli5: If one road is wide and another is narrow, it makes sense to send more cars down the wide one. This gives each road a sign with its size.

sections.title: The Community Format
sections.content:
The community is an 8-octet extended community. The high-order octet of the Type field is 0x00 for the transitive form or 0x40 for the non-transitive form, and the low-order octet (the SubType) MUST be 0x04, meaning link-bandwidth.

The Global Administrator sub-field is 2 octets. It SHOULD hold the Autonomous System Number (ASN) of the router attaching the community, but it MAY hold any 2-octet value. If the ASN does not fit in 2 octets, AS_TRANS (RFC 6793) SHOULD be used; 4-octet ASNs are not supported. This value does not affect the semantics of the community.

The Local Administrator sub-field holds the bandwidth as a 4-octet IEEE 754 floating point number. The unit is bytes per second, not bits.
sections.eli5: The sign has a type tag, a label saying who put it up, and the number that really matters: how much traffic the road can carry per second.

sections.title: What the Sender Does
sections.content:
A BGP speaker that attaches the community SHOULD be able to send either variant, and implementations SHOULD let operators configure the transitivity and the Global Administrator and bandwidth values through local policy. Defaults may differ between implementations, and implementations SHOULD expose their default.

A sender MAY advertise a bandwidth of zero, for example to signal that a path should not attract traffic during maintenance. Normally one community of the desired transitivity is attached to a route, but during a transition a speaker MAY attach one of each, and their bandwidth values SHOULD be the same. The community may be attached or updated on receipt (Adj-RIB-In) or when advertising to a neighbor (Adj-RIB-Out).
sections.eli5: The router that puts up the sign can choose which kind of sign to use and even say zero, which means please do not send cars here right now.

sections.title: What the Receiver Does
sections.content:
A receiver that supports the community MUST process both variants. It MUST NOT flap the session or treat the route as malformed because of the community's transitivity or because the session is internal or external. Implementations MAY provide configuration to accept non-transitive communities from external sessions.

A bandwidth of zero is valid. When every contributing path has a non-zero value, the values (or their ratio) can serve as weights for weighted load-balancing. If values are a mix of zero and non-zero, or all zero, local policy decides. Examples are excluding the zero paths, or falling back to equal load-balancing. The bandwidth value SHOULD NOT be used as input to BGP best path selection. If the two variants carry the same value, transitivity does not matter for computing weights or programming the forwarding table.
sections.eli5: A router that reads the signs shares traffic in proportion to the numbers. If the numbers do not make sense, it follows its own house rules.

sections.title: Passing the Community Along
sections.content:
When a speaker re-advertises a route and changes the next hop (to itself or another address), it MAY, as its default, remove the community, pass it on unchanged, or regenerate it with an updated value. Implementations SHOULD allow this to be changed per session and SHOULD expose the default. A regenerated community follows the sender procedures.

If the next hop is not changed, as when a route is re-advertised or reflected, the speaker SHOULD NOT change the community in any way.

In a BGP multipath setting, the value that is sent MAY be calculated from the communities on each contributing path. The RFC leaves how to do this out of scope and points to a separate use-cases document.
sections.eli5: When a route is handed on to someone new, the router may keep the sign, throw it away, or write a fresh one. If it hands it on without changing anything, it must not touch the sign.

sections.title: Error Handling
sections.content:
If a route carries more than one Link Bandwidth Extended Community and is used for weighted load-balancing, the speaker SHOULD use the one with the lowest bandwidth value, including zero, ignoring transitivity. Implementations MAY offer configuration to change this.

A negative value SHOULD NOT be attached or originated. A receiver that sees a negative value ignores the community. A community with a zero value MUST NOT be considered malformed. If any path lacks a valid community, equal load-balancing SHOULD be used unless local configuration says otherwise.
sections.eli5: If two signs disagree, believe the smallest number. If a sign makes no sense or is missing, share traffic evenly.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The extension has similar security implications to BGP extended communities in general. The community also conveys bandwidth and capacity information that may be sensitive, and exporting it outside an administrative domain can reveal private network resource details. When routes are sent toward an untrusted network or beyond the administrative domain, operators are advised to use policy to filter this community out.
sections.eli5: The sign tells how big your roads are, which is private. Do not show it to strangers.

sections.title: Operational Considerations
sections.content:
Earlier deployments of this feature used implementations that understood only one of the two transitivity types and ignored the other. In a mixed network, a speaker may update only one of two communities on a route, leaving the other with an inconsistent value, and downstream speakers may then do inappropriate weighted load-balancing. Operators who know older implementations are present can filter the unsupported type when advertising from the older speaker, or have a receiver strip the type the sender cannot handle. The RFC describes this as ideally short lived, until all routers are upgraded.

The Appendix notes that the earliest drafts supported only the non-transitive form, and that upgrading only the route reflector does not give full interoperability. How the bandwidth value is determined is out of scope, but implementations are encouraged to limit the churn from frequently changing values, since rapid fluctuations could affect protocol stability.
sections.eli5: If some routers read only one kind of sign, they can get confused. Upgrade them all, and do not keep changing the number too often.

fields.name: Global Administrator
fields.desc: Operator-assigned 2-octet value, for example a 16-bit ASN.

fields.name: Local Administrator
fields.desc: Bandwidth in bytes per second as a 32-bit IEEE 754 float.
